7YMbnciQHjA.title: Post-Eid Plans: Daring to Change
7YMbnciQHjA.one_line: After Ramadan: Muslims have ideals but lack buy-in; small committed growth in rituals, learning and volunteering by a few can change everyone.
7YMbnciQHjA.summary: A week after Eid he takes stock of the month. Waiting in his car for Canada geese to cross, he reflects that in the places he grew up drivers might have run them over, despite abundant Islamic teaching on mercy to animals. Muslims have flawless ideals; what is missing is buy-in. The Prophet built Islam not on the crowd at the Farewell Sermon but on a small group who held themselves to his standard, and he holds a two percent theory: if that share of a population actually lives what everyone claims to believe, the rest follow. Allah does not change a people until they change themselves. The post-Eid slump is natural, he says, because Ramadan was Allah opening His doors, not our own strength; it was a taste, like a Costco sample, meant to start lasting change. The Prophet left scholars, not amateurs, which is why Islam survived his death. In the second khutbah he gives three areas for modest growth: rituals, such as three fasts a month, daily dhikr and a little Quran with reflection; serious, sustained learning with a teacher instead of short videos and couch opinions, since poorly answered questions drive youth from Islam; and volunteering one's time, expertise or wealth, because Allah is served through serving His creation.

outline.heading: Opening
Geese on the road: the teaching is not what's missing
outline.gist: After rendering the verse on seeking help through patience and prayer, he describes stopping for Canada geese and how drivers where he grew up might have run them over, though Islamic teaching on mercy to animals is abundant.

outline.heading: What's missing is buy-in
outline.gist: Muslims have the best ideals, principles and ethics, fully explained, modelled and rewarded. Nothing is wrong with them; what is missing is the buy-in.

outline.heading: The Prophet built Islam on a committed few
outline.gist: Islam was not built on the hundred thousand at the Farewell Sermon, many of whom withheld zakat after his death, but on a small group who held themselves to his standard. A population cannot follow one person alone; it needs a group of examples.

outline.heading: The two percent theory
outline.gist: To change a population you need only two percent who hold themselves to the standard everyone claims to believe in, in business, family and how they earn. Without that buy-in, khutbahs are just talk.

outline.heading: Allah does not change a people until they change themselves
outline.gist: Ar-Ra'd 13:11 is quoted so often it has become a cliche, but nothing changes until change occurs: either we change, or we live with the consequences of long stagnation.

outline.heading: Ramadan was about Allah, not us
outline.gist: A week after Eid he is the same person but feels different, which shows Ramadan was never about his strength: Allah opened His doors and said come to Me. Feeling the difference now is normal because those doors are no longer open the same way.

outline.heading: A taste of what can be
outline.gist: Ramadan is not an open buffet but a taste, like a sample at Costco: here is how beautiful closeness to Allah is. You can keep some degree of it if a few things change.

outline.heading: Ramadan as a jump-start for the two percent
outline.gist: Ramadan is meant to jump-start continuous change, not be a seasonal novelty. If two percent carry it forward and enjoy it at a higher level, others follow, as drivers start stopping for animals once a few do; culture moves people more than law.

outline.heading: The Prophet left scholars, not amateurs
outline.gist: Each year the community should start higher. The Prophet left people able to carry the ummah without him, which is why most of us, not from Quraysh, are Muslim today, and why Islam survived the greatest loss when organizations collapse with their leaders.

outline.heading: Interlude
Category one, rituals: fasting and dhikr
outline.gist: You cannot keep Ramadan's pace, so add something sustainable: three fasts a month, ideally the 13th to 15th, and a set daily amount of dhikr to keep Allah's name on your tongue.

outline.heading: A daily portion of Quran with reflection
outline.gist: Do not let 24 hours pass without reading something of the book of Allah, even a few lines, and take a few minutes to think about what you read.

outline.heading: One step forward: audit your routine
outline.gist: Come to the masjid more often, write down honestly what you do for dhikr, Quran and prayer, and add one thing, perhaps Monday and Thursday. Walk toward Allah and He comes running to you.

outline.heading: Category two: real knowledge takes commitment
outline.gist: The ummah was built and saved by knowledge, and its lack is our number one problem. It does not come from five-minute videos or between Netflix commercials; commit to a weekly lesson, a course with an assessment, and a teacher.

outline.heading: A scholar is not good only when he agrees with you
outline.gist: Real learning means committing to someone for decades. People judge a sheikh by whether he agrees with them and look for another when he does not; neither the imam nor you is the standard of knowledge.

outline.heading: Poor answers drive children from Islam
outline.gist: Nothing is a higher priority than learning Islam properly and making sure your children do. A child given an answer that made no sense carries it for years and may leave Islam; after twenty years no one can undo it.

outline.heading: Category three: find your piece of the puzzle
outline.gist: Whether seven or seventy, find what you will offer the ummah: pro bono work, helping masajid, outreach, dawah or mentorship. Earning for your family has reward, but more is needed.

outline.heading: Time, expertise or wealth: Allah blesses what you offer
outline.gist: Everyone has something to give, even if it is not flashy; offer it and Allah puts barakah in it. Seek small, lasting growth in all three categories, not one.

outline.heading: Serve Allah by serving His creation
outline.gist: Allah needs no service, so He channelled service to Him through service to people. The minbar is overrated; many other doors of service are more profound and last longer.

outline.heading: The slump shows how strong Allah's call was
outline.gist: Feeling less connected and making mistakes this week is normal; it shows how powerful Allah's call was that we committed for 30 days. Rather than wait eleven months, change a little and get some of it back.

outline.heading: Outro

57:7.ar: ءَامِنُواْ بِٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ وَأَنفِقُواْ مِمَّا جَعَلَكُم مُّسۡتَخۡلَفِينَ فِيهِۖ فَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ مِنكُمۡ وَأَنفَقُواْ لَهُمۡ أَجۡرࣱ كَبِيرࣱ‏
57:7.en: Believe in Allah and His messenger, and spend of that whereof He hath made you trustees; and such of you as believe and spend (aright), theirs will be a great reward

57:8.ar: وَمَا لَكُمۡ لَا تُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلرَّسُولُ يَدۡعُوكُمۡ لِتُؤۡمِنُواْ بِرَبِّكُمۡ وَقَدۡ أَخَذَ مِيثَٰقَكُمۡ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤۡمِنِينَ
57:8.en: What aileth you that ye believe not in Allah, when the messenger calleth you to believe in your Lord, and He hath already made a covenant with you, if ye are believers

57:9.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِي يُنَزِّلُ عَلَىٰ عَبۡدِهِۦٓ ءَايَٰتِۭ بَيِّنَٰتࣲ لِّيُخۡرِجَكُم مِّنَ ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ إِلَى ٱلنُّورِۚ وَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِكُمۡ لَرَءُوفࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
57:9.en: He it is Who sendeth down clear revelations unto His slave, that He may bring you forth from darkness unto light; and lo! for you, Allah is Full of Pity, Merciful

57:10.ar: وَمَا لَكُمۡ أَلَّا تُنفِقُواْ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ وَلِلَّهِ مِيرَٰثُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۚ لَا يَسۡتَوِي مِنكُم مَّنۡ أَنفَقَ مِن قَبۡلِ ٱلۡفَتۡحِ وَقَٰتَلَۚ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ أَعۡظَمُ دَرَجَةࣰ مِّنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَنفَقُواْ مِنۢ بَعۡدُ وَقَٰتَلُواْۚ وَكُلࣰّ ا وَعَدَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلۡحُسۡنَىٰۚ وَٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ خَبِيرࣱ‏
57:10.en: And what aileth you that ye spend not in the way of Allah when unto Allah belongeth the inheritance of the heavens and the earth? Those who spent and fought before the victory are not upon a level (with the rest of you). Such are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterwards. Unto each hath Allah promised good. And Allah is Informed of what ye do

57:11.ar: مَّن ذَا ٱلَّذِي يُقۡرِضُ ٱللَّهَ قَرۡضًا حَسَنࣰ ا فَيُضَٰعِفَهُۥ لَهُۥ وَلَهُۥٓ أَجۡرࣱ كَرِيمࣱ‏
57:11.en: Who is he that will lend unto Allah a goodly loan, that He may double it for him and his may be a rich reward

57:1.ar: سَبَّحَ لِلَّهِ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ وَهُوَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
57:1.en: All that is in the heavens and the earth glorifieth Allah; and He is the Mighty, the Wise

57:2.ar: لَهُۥ مُلۡكُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ يُحۡيِۦ وَيُمِيتُۖ وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ قَدِيرٌ
57:2.en: His is the Sovereignty of the heavens and the earth; He quickeneth and He giveth death; and He is Able to do all things

57:3.ar: هُوَ ٱلۡأَوَّلُ وَٱلۡأٓخِرُ وَٱلظَّٰهِرُ وَٱلۡبَاطِنُۖ وَهُوَ بِكُلِّ شَيۡءٍ عَلِيمٌ
57:3.en: He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward; and He is Knower of all things

57:4.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ فِي سِتَّةِ أَيَّامࣲ ثُمَّ ٱسۡتَوَىٰ عَلَى ٱلۡعَرۡشِۖ يَعۡلَمُ مَا يَلِجُ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَمَا يَخۡرُجُ مِنۡهَا وَمَا يَنزِلُ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَمَا يَعۡرُجُ فِيهَاۖ وَهُوَ مَعَكُمۡ أَيۡنَ مَا كُنتُمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ بَصِيرࣱ‏
57:4.en: He it is Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days; then He mounted the Throne. He knoweth all that entereth the earth and all that emergeth therefrom and all that cometh down from the sky and all that ascendeth therein; and He is with you wheresoever ye may be. And Allah is Seer of what ye do

57:5.ar: لَّهُۥ مُلۡكُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۚ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ تُرۡجَعُ ٱلۡأُمُورُ
57:5.en: His is the Sovereignty of the heavens and the earth, and unto Allah (all) things are brought back

57:6.ar: يُولِجُ ٱلَّيۡلَ فِي ٱلنَّهَارِ وَيُولِجُ ٱلنَّهَارَ فِي ٱلَّيۡلِۚ وَهُوَ عَلِيمُۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ
57:6.en: He causeth the night to pass into the day, and He causeth the day to pass into the night, and He is knower of all that is in the breasts

7:172.ar: وَإِذۡ أَخَذَ رَبُّكَ مِنۢ بَنِيٓ ءَادَمَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمۡ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمۡ وَأَشۡهَدَهُمۡ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمۡ أَلَسۡتُ بِرَبِّكُمۡۖ قَالُواْ بَلَىٰ شَهِدۡنَآۚ أَن تَقُولُواْ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ إِنَّا كُنَّا عَنۡ هَٰذَا غَٰفِلِينَ
7:172.en: And (remember) when thy Lord brought forth from the Children of Adam, from their reins, their seed, and made them testify of themselves, (saying): Am I not your Lord? They said: Yea, verily. We testify. (That was) lest ye should say at the Day of Resurrection: Lo! of this we were unaware

yRz5XTGN3m0.title: Tafseer of Surat al-Hadid, Part 3: Verses 7-11
yRz5XTGN3m0.one_line: Verses 7-11 pair belief with giving from all we are entrusted with, arguing the community most needs members' time, wisdom and commitment.
yRz5XTGN3m0.summary: After recapping the cluster of choices from Qaf to al-Hadid, he reads verse 7 as the surah's thesis: belief, which he defines as a profound acknowledgment that produces matching behaviour, joined with spending from whatever Allah has made us stewards of. Because the verse avoids the word wealth, he argues that Muslims in the West most need to give time, knowledge and wisdom: a minority facing opposing values cannot survive with a handful of overworked imams, children need other adults to validate the values their parents teach, boys need role models and standards, and minorities historically dissolve within a few generations unless they build working systems. He asks each listener to find their own piece and commit to it for life. Verse 8 gives two reasons to believe, the Messenger calling with evidence and the primordial covenant within, and he notes no one is accountable without receiving the message. Verse 9 describes revelation as enlightenment, which leads him to warn against obsessing over mechanics while neglecting presence. Verse 10's argument for giving is that everything already belongs to Allah, and those who give when faith is hard outrank those who give when it is easy. Verse 11 invites a goodly loan that Allah multiplies.

outline.heading: Opening
Memorize and understand the last quarter of the Quran
outline.gist: The final four parts condense the Quran's values; memorizing and understanding them gives a solid Islamic foundation.

outline.heading: The cluster of choices from Qaf to al-Waqi'ah
outline.gist: Each surah offers a stark choice: righteousness or falsehood, purpose or aimlessness, guidance, certainty, gratitude, and which of the three groups to join on the Day of Judgment, where worldly categories vanish.

outline.heading: Al-Hadid: the right mix of both
outline.gist: Unlike the earlier surahs, al-Hadid demands a balance of spirituality and materialism, introduced through descriptions of Allah that look like opposites.

outline.heading: What iman really means
outline.gist: Iman is not mere belief but a profound acknowledgment of a principle that leads to behaviour reflecting it.

outline.heading: Spend from what He made you steward of
outline.gist: The unique wording points to khilafah: health, knowledge, time and compassion are on loan, to be spent for the purpose He set.

outline.heading: Time and wisdom before money
outline.gist: In the West, time has little barakah and the next generation faces confusing ethical dilemmas, so what our community needs most is time, knowledge and wisdom.

outline.heading: A minority needs many more workers
outline.gist: A million Canadian Muslims facing opposing values cannot be served by a few imams who burn out; the people needed are already in the room.

outline.heading: Parents cannot be everything to their children
outline.gist: Most service needs no scholarship, only availability and decency; a parent cannot also be a child's friend and mentor, so others must step in.

outline.heading: Boys need role models and standards
outline.gist: Without standards and present fathers boys drift into passivity; the Prophet raised the young by holding them to standards, never by force.

outline.heading: Children need outside validation of their values
outline.gist: Children test whether their parents are normal; when other adults reinforce the same values they hold, and when they contradict them the child disconnects. A close-knit community lightens that load.

outline.heading: Our values are a trust, or they dissolve
outline.gist: The values we carry are part of what we are stewards of; many minority faiths disappeared within generations, and adherence can fall from 80 to 20 percent in four.

outline.heading: Accountable for a working system: presence over money
outline.gist: We answer for building a system that can last; organizations asking only for money has desensitized people, but what is short is commitment and presence.

outline.heading: Find your piece and commit for life
outline.gist: He will keep explaining verses until old age; each person must work out what they are good at and contribute it, since money alone needs a workforce.

outline.heading: Interlude
Recitation note: merging the tanween
outline.gist: A tajweed point on fully merging the nun sound of the tanween into the following letter, a common mistake.

outline.heading: The Messenger calling you to your Lord
outline.gist: The first, physical reason to believe: a Prophet among you explaining the evidence.

outline.heading: Four sources of iman and the hunger for meaning
outline.gist: Universe, life and history are external evidence; the fourth is inner experience, a universal craving for meaning whose denial breeds despair.

outline.heading: The covenant: 'Am I not your Lord?'
outline.gist: A spiritual engagement every soul affirmed; distractions only make that inner part hungrier, which is why the idea of God exists in every culture.

outline.heading: No accountability without the message
outline.gist: Someone never reached by the call is not held accountable for disbelief, like a person living on a mountain the Prophet never visited.

outline.heading: The spirit starves without Allah
outline.gist: Just as the body needs food, the spirit needs Allah; balance belief and practice, the material and the spiritual.

outline.heading: Clear signs to bring you into enlightenment
outline.gist: Physical signs serve a spiritual end: reading the universe and life moves people from darkness to enlightenment, a sign of Allah's tenderness.

outline.heading: We have lost clarity on what matters
outline.gist: Arguments and questions show how little we distinguish primary from tertiary matters; always ask how important something is before investing in it.

outline.heading: The Syrian scholar and the hands in prayer
outline.gist: A scholar told two groups arguing over hand placement to put their hands in their pockets so long as their hearts were with Allah; mechanics matter, but presence must get equal investment.

outline.heading: Any approach that drops one piece fails
outline.gist: Know how to recite and also understand; overrating either mechanics or spirit ruins practice.

outline.heading: Interlude
Why won't you spend? Allah inherits everything
outline.gist: The argument for giving is ownership: everything in the heavens and earth is His, so spend it as He directs.

outline.heading: The old man who sold him his house
outline.gist: An elderly seller told him to enjoy the house because it passes quickly; in a century none of us will own anything.

outline.heading: Even knowledge and memory are on loan
outline.gist: Allah can take a person's memory in an instant, as geriatric patients show; even what is in our minds is not ours.

outline.heading: Before the victory: when Islam is hard
outline.gist: He now reads the 'fath' as general rather than a later Madinan insertion: those who give and stand firm before things become easy rank higher, and being Muslim today is hard.

outline.heading: Equal gifts, unequal reward
outline.gist: Two people giving the same amount are not equal if one gave in hardship; al-Khabir knows the inner difficulty that the senses cannot reach.

outline.heading: Hijab and prayer at work when it costs you
outline.gist: Wearing hijab or praying openly where it threatens one's career earns far more than doing so where it is welcomed.

outline.heading: Measured both materially and spiritually
outline.gist: A jurist can only judge wudu and qiblah; Allah also judges presence, and may decline a prayer done while thinking of food.

outline.heading: A goodly loan to Allah
outline.gist: Allah frames giving as a loan He repays manifold, growing it as one raises a foal into a horse.

themes.label: Giving from what you are entrusted with
themes.note: Spending covers time, wisdom, knowledge and values, not only money; the community's shortage is people who commit.

themes.label: Building a committed community

3KW_FQEA8rY.title: Attributes of the Prophet: How He Treated Us
3KW_FQEA8rY.one_line: The Prophet's care for his future ummah: the Quran he left, the ease he chose for us, his tears, his longing, and his intercession.
3KW_FQEA8rY.summary: After many sessions on how the Prophet treated those around him, he turns to how the Prophet treated us, the believers who came later. He starts from the verse reminding believers that the Messenger is among them and the condition of accepting his judgement wholeheartedly. The Prophet's legacy was the Quran, a rope between us and Allah, and a path left clear as day; losing him was the ummah's greatest calamity, yet he left everything needed. He then gathers evidence that the Prophet thought of us in his choices: making dua for his ummah in every prayer, saving his one guaranteed dua for intercession, refraining from commanding siwak or nightly congregational prayer in Ramadan, and discouraging questions so the religion would stay flexible for later contexts. He describes the Prophet weeping over his ummah when reciting the prayers of Ibrahim and Isa, Allah's promise to satisfy him, his longing for brothers he never met, the image of believers recognised by their shining limbs, and his waiting for them at the Basin. He ends with the great intercession, where he repeatedly asks for his nation and enters Paradise only after them, and asks listeners to love him back, at least by sending him salawat.

outline.heading: Opening
The Messenger is among you
outline.gist: Having covered how he treated his companions, family and others, he turns to how he treats us; in many ways the Prophet is still present among believers.

outline.heading: Accepting his judgement wholeheartedly
outline.gist: Faith is not complete until people accept his rulings and find no resistance in their hearts.

outline.heading: The Quran as a rope to Allah
outline.gist: His legacy was the Quran, a rope with one end in Allah's hand and the other in ours; drop it and you have nothing.

outline.heading: The farewell admonition: a path clear as day
outline.gist: When companions sensed he was leaving, he told them he left them on a clear path whose night is like its day; only those who deviate are lost.

outline.heading: Losing him: the ummah's greatest calamity
outline.gist: No disaster has struck the ummah worse than his death, and anyone who truly loves him feels this, but he did not leave before giving us what we need.

outline.heading: The dua for Aisha he makes for his ummah
outline.gist: He made a dua for Aisha's complete forgiveness, and when she rejoiced he told her he makes it for his ummah in every prayer.

outline.heading: Saving his one guaranteed dua for intercession
outline.gist: Every prophet had one dua sure to be answered and used it in this world; he saved his for his ummah on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Commands he withheld to spare us: siwak and nightly Ramadan prayer
outline.gist: He would have ordered siwak with every prayer and led the night prayer every night, but held back lest they become obligations too hard for later Muslims.

outline.heading: Discouraging questions to keep the deen flexible
outline.gist: Answers given to one context would have bound later generations, so he discouraged questions to preserve the religion's room to move.

outline.heading: Weeping over the prayers of Ibrahim and Isa
outline.gist: He recited the two prophets' pleas for those who did not follow them, raised his hands and wept for his ummah.

outline.heading: Allah will satisfy you regarding your ummah
outline.gist: Jibril was sent to tell him Allah would please him concerning his nation and not grieve him, the sense of the promise in Ad-Duha.

outline.heading: Ta Ha: stand with both feet on the ground
outline.gist: A reading of the opening letters of Ta Ha as a command to plant his feet, since he stood so long on his toes in prayer for his ummah.

outline.heading: Longing for brothers he never met
outline.gist: Visiting the martyrs of Uhud, he wished he could see his brothers: the believers who would come after and believe without seeing him.

outline.heading: Known by shining limbs
outline.gist: He will recognise his ummah as a man recognises his white-blazed horses among dark ones, by the light of their ablution.

outline.heading: Meet me at the Basin
outline.gist: He goes ahead to wait at the Hawd, and those who did not deviate drink from his hand; his recurring phrase was that our appointment is at the Basin, so do not be late.

outline.heading: Those who believe without seeing him
outline.gist: Asked whether anyone would be better than the companions, he spoke of later believers who would give up family and wealth to sit with him; some will love him more than some who saw him.

outline.heading: The great intercession beneath the Throne
outline.gist: People go from prophet to prophet seeking intercession; he prostrates and praises Allah in words never said before until told to raise his head and ask.

outline.heading: My nation, my nation
outline.gist: His first words are for his ummah, and he returns again and again to intercede until only those the Quran holds back remain; all humanity after him is his nation.

outline.heading: He enters Paradise after us
outline.gist: He makes sure those he intercedes for enter before him: he cried for us, gave us a clear and flexible way of life and hoped to meet us.

outline.heading: Loving him back with salawat
outline.gist: Whoever sends him salam, Allah returns his soul so he replies; the least we can do is show him love in return.

4:3.en: And if ye fear that ye will not deal fairly by the orphans, marry of the women, who seem good to you, two or three or four; and if ye fear that ye cannot do justice (to so many) then one (only) or (the captives) that your right hands possess. 4:11.en: Allah chargeth you concerning (the provision for) your children: to the male the equivalent of the portion of two females, and if there be women more than two, then theirs is two-thirds of the inheritance, and if there be one (only) then the half. aDXlooe2FWU.title: Facing Disbelief 7: Violence, Freedoms, Women in Islam, and the Fourth Source of Iman: You
aDXlooe2FWU.one_line: Answers on Islam and violence, apostasy, Banu Qurayzah, personal freedom, slavery, hijab, polygamy, inheritance, 4:34 and Aisha, then the self as the fourth source of iman.
aDXlooe2FWU.summary: In the closing session he addresses challenges Muslims face about Islam itself. Islam was not spread by the sword: conquest was political, conquered peoples kept their faiths, and the worst abuses came centuries later. The executions in the Prophet's time targeted people actively raising armies or killing Muslims, never anyone for words alone, and the apostasy ruling concerned political betrayal; Abu Bakr fought tribes for withholding zakat. He argues the Banu Qurayzah numbers were inflated and the ruling came from the Torah. Combat verses are few and contextual, the 'commanded to fight people' hadith refers to specific tribes, and ISIS no more represents Islam than the KKK represents Christianity. On freedoms, he criticizes a culture that sanctifies the self over the community and warns that unsolicited public advice drives wavering people away. Islam ended slavery by drying up its sources and opening exits. Hijab answers the reality that men are visually oriented and demands that a woman be heard rather than judged. Polygamy was restricted, inheritance follows financial responsibility, 4:34 concerns infidelity and limits harmful speech, and Aisha's marriage fit its time. Finally, the self is the fourth source of iman: inner emptiness, the mind and lived experience all point to one Creator, and certainty built on facts fuels excellence.

outline.heading: Four sources of iman and two remaining challenges
outline.gist: Universe, life and history are covered; violence and freedoms remain as challenges Muslims face about Islam itself.

outline.heading: Islam was not spread by the sword
outline.gist: Conquest was political border-securing; conquered people chose their faith, which is why the Middle East still has many religious communities.

outline.heading: Later abuses and the fall of Andalusia
outline.gist: Brutal wars came centuries later and are human history, not Islam, while Muslims in Andalusia were forcibly converted or killed.

outline.heading: Executions in the Prophet's time: no dictating to a prophet
outline.gist: We cannot set our own picture of what a prophet must do and judge him by it.

outline.heading: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf
outline.gist: He funded war, plotted assassinations and helped assemble the Confederates; most leaders would have acted years earlier.

outline.heading: Abu Rafi' Sallam
outline.gist: He financed mercenaries; only he was executed and his family was untouched.

outline.heading: Khalid ibn Sufyan al-Hudhali
outline.gist: He was raising an army to raid Madinah, and it dispersed after his death.

outline.heading: Umm Qirfa
outline.gist: A powerful woman protected by fifty swords who killed Muslims and attempted the Prophet's life.

outline.heading: Names at the conquest of Makkah
outline.gist: Those named had murdered Muslims in peacetime; all fled and were later pardoned.

outline.heading: No one was executed for words alone
outline.gist: Every authentic case involved murder or war-making; weakly narrated cases need no defence.

outline.heading: Apostasy as political betrayal
outline.gist: Other narrations tie the ruling to leaving the community and fighting it, the Quran sets no such penalty, and some imams held it ended with the Prophet.

outline.heading: Abu Bakr's wars were about zakat
outline.gist: Most tribes did not leave Islam; they refused to send zakat to the central treasury.

outline.heading: Banu Qurayzah: treaty and betrayal
outline.gist: They broke a citizenship pact by opening the way to the Confederates during the trench.

outline.heading: Banu Qurayzah: where the large numbers came from
outline.gist: Estimates range from forty to nine hundred; the high figures come from a narrator of that tribe, and Jewish chronicles record no such massacre.

outline.heading: Banu Qurayzah: the house and the Torah ruling
outline.gist: No house could hold hundreds, and Sa'd ruled by the Torah's law on wartime betrayal, not the Quran.

outline.heading: Banu Qurayzah: a likelier count
outline.gist: Perhaps sixty or seventy armed men; mass executions and graves on that scale left no trace, and Arab narrators are loose with numbers.

outline.heading: Combat in the Quran is limited and contextual
outline.gist: About twenty-five verses in a handful of surahs, beginning with fighting those who fight you without transgressing.

outline.heading: Peace when the enemy inclines to peace
outline.gist: The Prophet kept renewing treaties others broke, until Surat al-Tawbah gave the treaty-breaking tribes four months.

outline.heading: 'I was commanded to fight the people'
outline.gist: Extremists' favourite hadith refers to the specific pagan tribes of Surat al-Tawbah, not humanity.

outline.heading: The claim that one verse abrogates over a hundred
outline.gist: Extremists cut a political verse about Rome and Persia from its context to cancel every verse of tolerance.

outline.heading: ISIS does not represent Islam
outline.gist: Every ideology has a radical arm; these groups were armed, funded and amplified, and if two billion Muslims believed this nothing would remain.

outline.heading: Freedoms and the social contract
outline.gist: Islam puts the group's interest above the individual's while keeping basic freedoms; modern liberalism has reversed this.

outline.heading: The culture of entitlement
outline.gist: People accept fines for littering yet reject God's guidance; self-celebration is producing weak, selfish people.

outline.heading: Gender debates as a sign of decline
outline.gist: Sanctifying the self drives current gender arguments, which historians link to declining, wealthy civilizations like Rome and Persia.

outline.heading: Interlude
The man at the bus stop
outline.gist: A stranger's advice about a haircut can push someone on the edge out of Islam for good.

outline.heading: Conditions for giving advice
outline.gist: Advice needs a relationship, three days of reflection, and an issue that is fundamental and not a matter of scholarly difference.

outline.heading: We educate, we do not control
outline.gist: Acting as guardians of Islam pushes away people in the grey zone; how one practises is one's own choice.

outline.heading: Slavery: drying up its sources
outline.gist: Slavery predated Islam and was not racial in Arabia; Islam closed debt and other routes, leaving only war captives.

outline.heading: Slavery: opening the exits
outline.gist: Freeing slaves as reward and expiation, obligatory buy-out agreements, and automatic freedom for a mother of a free man's child.

outline.heading: Why not abolish by decree
outline.gist: An economic institution cannot be ended by one ruling; Islam set up a system to phase it out.

outline.heading: Freed slaves who asked to return
outline.gist: Without connections or support, many could not survive, and Islam gave slaves rights they never had before.

outline.heading: American slavery was a different institution
outline.gist: Racial, imported and denied all rights, so it had to end through war, unlike the Muslim world where numbers dwindled.

outline.heading: Men are visually oriented
outline.gist: A fact of biology, shown by social media fame, OnlyFans and pornography; we must deal with what is, not what should be.

outline.heading: Hijab demands to be heard, not looked at
outline.gist: Covering refuses objectification and is an issue of identity and respect.

outline.heading: Who wins when women uncover
outline.gist: Men were handed what they always wanted for free, which is no victory for women.

outline.heading: A system for chastity, as workplaces now admit
outline.gist: No one may ever be harassed whatever they wear; dress and conduct codes like those at work protect everyone.

outline.heading: Polygamy was restricted, not introduced
outline.gist: Islam cut unlimited marriage to four, with justice required, and one spouse as the norm.

outline.heading: The right to a monogamy clause; Ali and Fatimah
outline.gist: Women could stipulate no second wife, and Ali married no one else while Fatimah lived.

outline.heading: Inheritance: women often receive more
outline.gist: Many cases give women equal or greater shares; only the sibling case troubles people.

outline.heading: Inheritance follows financial responsibility
outline.gist: Men must support the women in their lives while a woman's wealth is entirely hers.

outline.heading: 4:34 is about infidelity
outline.gist: The verse concerns letting an unwanted man into the home; the steps begin with a gentle, loving reminder.

outline.heading: Verbal abuse is worse than physical
outline.gist: Harsh words scar for life, so speech is limited and the husband leaves the room.

outline.heading: The final step and abuse of the verse
outline.gist: The Prophet never struck a woman; the step is a symbolic gesture to save a marriage with children, and a bruise shown to a judge means jail.

outline.heading: Aisha's marriage in its context
outline.gist: Early marriage was normal; she had been engaged before, and his own great-grandparents married at thirteen and twelve.

outline.heading: Her age and her own testimony
outline.gist: Her age may have been older, but either way she became the greatest narrator of his beauty and love; judging it by today is the historian's fallacy.

outline.heading: The fourth source of iman: your inner emptiness
outline.gist: Nothing fills the void inside, a reminder of a power beyond you that wants you.

outline.heading: The mind as evidence
outline.gist: A mind that thinks about thinking cannot come from something lesser than itself.

outline.heading: Personal experience of being rescued
outline.gist: He has seen Allah bail him out again and again through hardship, giving meaning and fulfilment.

outline.heading: Uniformity of the four sources
outline.gist: Universe, life, history and the self all point to one Creator, and only Islam's description of God, preserved text and Prophet fit.

outline.heading: Certainty fuels excellence
outline.gist: Removing doubt gives inner strength and attentiveness to Allah's commands; build faith on facts, not flimsy claims.

outline.heading: Outro

T9Ja-LMsEt8.title: Arabic Tafsir: Opening of Surat al-Saffat 37:1-11 (Obedience in the Unseen)
T9Ja-LMsEt8.one_line: Al-Saffat teaches obedience that accepts the unseen: an oath by the angels answered with 'your God is One', and the stars that guard heaven from devils.
T9Ja-LMsEt8.summary: He introduces al-Saffat within the cluster on obedience: after surahs on hardship, society, knowledge and true life, this one teaches that submission must include the unseen. Faith is not blind; it rests on four sources, the universe, life, history and the self, but science cannot reach the Creator, and once faith is settled one accepts commands whose wisdom stays hidden. He warns against leaving Islam over secondary questions and calls the claim to grasp every divine wisdom a form of arrogance. The surah opens with an oath unique to the Quran, by the angels standing in ranks, driving and reciting, about whom we know nothing beyond the text, and its answer is that your God is One. Tawhid matters because it gives morality one fixed source that no group can shift; a believer's values stay the same in every place and condition. The second passage says the lowest heaven is adorned with stars that also guard against devils who try to eavesdrop. He makes this the basis for a sharp campaign against jinn-blaming, magic-breaking and exorcism culture: keep daily ruqyah for your family, but stop blaming the unseen for every failure and drive charlatans out of the community.

outline.heading: Obedience, the great goal after faith
outline.gist: Once faith settles in the heart the aim is to obey Allah well; the cluster from al-Ahzab to al-Zumar examines obedience in depth.

outline.heading: Al-Ahzab and Saba: obeying in hardship, obeying as a society
outline.gist: Obedience in times of difficulty is the real test; Saba is unique in addressing the obedience of whole societies.

outline.heading: Fatir and Ya-Sin: knowledge and true life
outline.gist: Allah is obeyed as He wants, which needs knowledge; Ya-Sin shows obedience is the life of the spirit, which is why some are remembered for centuries and others forgotten.

outline.heading: Al-Saffat: obedience that includes the unseen
outline.gist: We cannot understand everything Allah commands; this is not blind following, which the Quran forbids, but acceptance once faith is established.

outline.heading: The four sources of faith, and what science cannot do
outline.gist: Faith comes from looking at the universe, life, history and the self; experimental science studies how things exist and cannot reach before or beyond time and space.

outline.heading: Allah Himself is unseen
outline.gist: All prophets brought the same message; if science could prove Allah He would no longer be unseen, so He is known through His work.

outline.heading: The unseen within creation: angels and jinn
outline.gist: Jinn see us and we do not see them, so photos of jinn are nonsense; people want to grasp everything by the senses, like those of Musa's people who demanded to see Allah.

outline.heading: Seeing Allah belongs to another realm
outline.gist: Allah is not perceived by the senses in this world; seeing Him in the Hereafter is affirmed, under laws we do not know.

outline.heading: Why this surah sits mid-cluster
outline.gist: Most commands come with reasons and evidence, but some of Allah's wisdom is hidden, and accepting it is part of faith.

outline.heading: Wisdom shown or not, the ruling stands
outline.gist: Pork is forbidden whether a million studies show harm or benefit; Allah is the wisest of judges, so known wisdom is good and unknown wisdom is also good.

outline.heading: A teacher must explain, a believer must accept
outline.gist: It is his duty to show the wisdom of every ruling he can, and a failing if he does not, but a believer does not choose once Allah and His Messenger decide.

outline.heading: Faith is not won or lost on secondary issues
outline.gist: People leave Islam over the number of rakaat, the Prophet's marriages or Aisha's age; these are branches, and the way back is to the sources of faith.

outline.heading: One set of laws, a beginning and an end
outline.gist: Some religious arguments rest on false science out of fear of atheism; a universe under one set of laws with a beginning needs a single law-giver.

outline.heading: Why does life want to live?
outline.gist: Every living thing resists death because whoever programmed life gave it that aim, and life cannot create itself.

outline.heading: The Quran says look, then accept
outline.gist: It points to sun, moon, mountains and past nations; once faith settles, you answer 'at your service' whether the wisdom appears or not.

outline.heading: Claiming every wisdom is arrogance
outline.gist: Believing your intelligence must grasp all of Allah's wisdom is pride; he seeks wisdom only to help people come to faith.

outline.heading: A middle-Meccan surah from the years of Dar al-Arqam
outline.gist: Meccan surahs of that phase built faith and submission in the companions who later stood with the Prophet; he begins the recitation.

outline.heading: The six-count madd in 'wa al-saffat'
outline.gist: A madd followed by a doubled letter within a word is always six counts, the longest in Hafs.

outline.heading: An oath unique to the Quran
outline.gist: Swearing by a feminine plural with a following noun was new to the Arabs; Allah only swears by something meaningful to the answer, and here He swears by the unseen.

outline.heading: Angels in ranks: and that is all we know
outline.gist: Most commentators say these are angels; why they line up, how many and where, no one knows.

outline.heading: Those who drive
outline.gist: They urge things to happen or stop as Allah commands, in ways hidden from us.

outline.heading: Prompting from angels, whispering from devils
outline.gist: Good and evil thoughts are placed in the heart; even if you sense them, you never see the angel or the devil behind them.

outline.heading: The night the unseen met the Prophet
outline.gist: Laylat al-Qadr is great because Jibril came in his true form with hundreds of wings; at the Mi'raj the Prophet saw him again, humbled like a worn saddle-cloth before Allah's majesty.

outline.heading: Those who recite: accept it as stated
outline.gist: They bring scripture to messengers; anyone who claims to describe the details of the angels' ranks, driving or recitation is lying.

outline.heading: The answer: your God is One
outline.gist: Lord of the heavens and earth and of the easts, the many points where the sun rises across the year.

outline.heading: Modern people no longer look at the sky
outline.gist: Ancient people tracked sun and moon; we rely on devices, and calculation for the month is a valid difference of opinion, but Islam tied prayer and fasting to the cosmos.

outline.heading: The small black box versus the great one
outline.gist: People stare down at phones instead of up at the night sky; a Quran full of cosmic signs moves those connected to them and loses force on a nation that is not.

outline.heading: Oneness is the easiest thing to show
outline.gist: The burden of proof is on whoever claims a second god; show me conflicting laws or a crack in the heavens.

outline.heading: A rare answer to an oath
outline.gist: Most Quranic oaths are answered with the Last Day, the Quran or the soul; few with tawhid, the one word that sums up Islam.

outline.heading: 'What difference does one god or three make?'
outline.gist: Some ask why it matters; on the Day people who argued with Allah over what happened to them fall silent when He shows them the reality.

outline.heading: Al-Khidr and the boy
outline.gist: Musa could not see why the boy was killed; Allah would give the parents someone better, and those who refuse His decree will see the reason on the Day and regret.

outline.heading: One source for the red lines
outline.gist: If people draw the line they can move it for a favour; with one God, no one can make the forbidden lawful, and zina is forbidden in every age, place and state, as for Yusuf.

outline.heading: Fixed values in every circumstance
outline.gist: Apart from Allah's own exceptions, a believer is truthful in strength and weakness and keeps his values on any planet or in any era, because their source does not change.

outline.heading: Circumstances change, values do not
outline.gist: Rich or poor, settled or displaced, sick or well, he stays merciful; under many gods or human committees the line shifts tomorrow.

outline.heading: No escape from Him except to Him
outline.gist: Because He is one, He commands and you obey, decrees and you accept; with two gods you could run from one to the other.

outline.heading: What lies between heaven and earth
outline.gist: There are hidden worlds between them, and 'the easts' may also mean the countless suns of other galaxies.

outline.heading: The vastness that unsettles astronomers
outline.gist: The scale of the universe leads some to insist we cannot be alone; Allah does create what we do not know, and only He tells us what exists.

outline.heading: Submission is accepting what He tells
outline.gist: You are not alone: there are jinn, angels and an unseen you know nothing of, and a believer accepts it whether seen or not.

outline.heading: Adorned with stars: a variant reading
outline.gist: Hafs reads 'bi-zinatin al-kawakib' with the stars in apposition, others read it as a possessive; he recites the passage.

outline.heading: The lowest heaven is all science can reach
outline.gist: Every heavenly body is a kawkab, stars included; the majority view is that the whole observable universe is the lowest heaven.

outline.heading: Bound by time and space
outline.gist: We cannot imagine anything free of time and place; other heavens may run on other laws.

outline.heading: Stars as protection from rebellious devils
outline.gist: A rebel is one who dares to do what is forbidden; the stars are beauty and signposts, and also a guard.

outline.heading: His lifelong fight against jinn and magic culture
outline.gist: He will keep speaking about Muslims' obsession with jinn, magic, sorcery and the evil eye, even if it annoys people.

outline.heading: Eavesdropping on the exalted assembly
outline.gist: Listening in on what you were not invited to hear differs from listening; no one has been to the exalted assembly to describe it.

outline.heading: Pelted from every side, and the piercing flame
outline.gist: Those who try are driven off with lasting punishment, and one who snatches a word is struck dead by a piercing flame.

outline.heading: Then why believe the charlatans?
outline.gist: After this, people still blame a charm under the pillow for failing to marry or have children, or for headaches.

outline.heading: The believer does not blame the unseen
outline.gist: Iblis blamed Allah for leading him astray; a believer looks for causes in this world and, if none is found, accepts the decree.

outline.heading: Do ruqyah for your family every day
outline.gist: He recites over himself, his wife and children daily and asks everyone to make it routine.

outline.heading: But stop blaming jinn for every failure
outline.gist: When someone falls ill or fails, do not come to him blaming magic; that is unacceptable in the religion.

outline.heading: The jinn found the sky full of guards
outline.gist: Surat al-Jinn has the jinn admit that heaven is filled with guards and flames since the Prophet's mission.

outline.heading: What Allah hid versus what you neglected
outline.gist: Rulings you never learned are your own failing, not the unseen; people leave what they should learn to chase what Allah hid.

outline.heading: Superstitions borrowed from other religions
outline.gist: Exorcism and magic-breaking have no basis in Islam; Allah protected us from them and we followed others span by span.

outline.heading: Do not probe how the unseen works
outline.gist: How jinn reach the sky or how flames strike them nobody knows; searching into it harms you and others.

outline.heading: People beaten until they truly lost their minds
outline.gist: Someone with a mental illness is convinced he is possessed and passed from one fraud to another; this culture must be uprooted, not changed gently.

outline.heading: Ask them: who is stronger in creation?
outline.gist: Are they harder to create than the stars, heaven, jinn and angels? Man was made from sticky clay, a wisdom for next week.

outline.heading: Outro

qFaEgB8_7Eg.title: The Five Categories of Community Investment
qFaEgB8_7Eg.one_line: Launching the series: the community lacks shared goals and commitment; the Prophet worked to clear goals, so here are five categories to invest in.
qFaEgB8_7Eg.summary: After ten years in the city, he says, the Muslim community runs around like a headless chicken: it has no clear goals and is really a population rather than a community, since nothing is centralized. People born here and immigrants who still call somewhere else home experience Islam differently, and both settle into a comfortable cycle of work and weekends that is not the Islamic way of life. The Prophet, by contrast, never moved aimlessly. At the second pledge of Aqabah he asked the people of Yathrib for five commitments: political allegiance, money, social and ethical reform, standing firm in battle, and protecting him as the bearer of revelation. At Hunayn he had the fleeing Muslims reminded of that pledge, and in Madinah he set and met goals: the masjid, the brotherhood between emigrants and Ansar, and the Constitution of Madinah. A survey he ran in 2018 showed needs but no shared vision. The deepest problem is commitment: people show up for two months then vanish, and Islam cannot be built part-time. Communal obligations matter as much as personal ones, and with no leadership structure everyone will answer for drugs, domestic violence and lost identity. In the second khutbah he outlines the five categories: education, mentorship, financial centralization, outreach and advocacy, and asks each person to find their piece.

outline.heading: Opening
Cooperate in righteousness
outline.gist: Al-Ma'idah's command to cooperate in righteousness and taqwa, not sin; his last Ramadan khutbah on following the Prophet proposed five categories of community investment, now a series.

outline.heading: Born here or arrived
outline.gist: After ten years here he sees that Muslims born and raised in Canada know only this experience of Islam and call it home, unlike those who came later.

outline.heading: A headless chicken
outline.gist: Immigrants still call somewhere else home, and these different experiences shape the solutions people seek; meanwhile the community has no clear goals and runs in circles.

outline.heading: A population, not yet a community
outline.gist: The goals were never discussed meaningfully; a community needs something centralized, whether politics, religion, finances or social life, and without it we are only a population.

outline.heading: Comfortable routine is not the Islamic way
outline.gist: Earning, vacations and weekends on repeat is not why Allah put us here; people need agreed categories for where to spend their time working toward something bigger than themselves.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet turned to Yathrib
outline.gist: Before the second pledge of Aqabah he was getting nowhere in Makkah without freedom to preach, so he approached tribes at Hajj and a few young men of Yathrib agreed.

outline.heading: He did not walk the earth aimlessly
outline.gist: He sent them back for more, twelve and then seventy-two with some women, and told them plainly the five things he needed: clear goals he worked to achieve.

outline.heading: Allegiance to a leader, not a consultant
outline.gist: Here every effort is whatever comes next with no common thread or measurable outcome; the Prophet's first demand was political allegiance to him as leader.

outline.heading: Wealth, and social and ethical reform
outline.gist: His goals fitted his context and ours will differ; he asked for financial commitment whatever one's means, and a commitment to reform oneself and society.

outline.heading: Standing firm, and protecting the bearer of the Quran
outline.gist: He needed them to hold their ground when battle came and to protect him as the one carrying the Quran, though he himself stood closest to the enemy.

outline.heading: Hunayn: remind them of the pledge
outline.gist: When the Muslims fled at Hunayn he had the call made to those who had pledged to him, and they returned; in Madinah he set goals, starting with the masjid and homes for the emigrants.

outline.heading: Brotherhood and the Constitution of Madinah
outline.gist: He paired emigrants with the Ansar and had every party sign the Constitution of Madinah, an underrated political masterpiece; commitments first, then goals achieved.

outline.heading: What are our goals? The 2018 survey
outline.gist: A thousand people answered his survey and the results were all over the place, agreeing on urgent needs, not on a vision.

outline.heading: Islam cannot be built part-time
outline.gist: Everywhere, the biggest obstacle is commitment: people get excited, show up for a month or two, vanish and return a year later.

outline.heading: The Prophet chose companions with grit
outline.gist: He has people with ideas and hope but little ability to commit; the Prophet chose those who would stand with him to the bitter end.

outline.heading: Find your piece of the puzzle
outline.gist: Faces appear for a while and fade; you cannot do everything, but you must find a niche among the community's goals and commit to it.

outline.heading: Communal obligations equal personal ones
outline.gist: Fard kifayah duties are as important as personal ones like Jumuah, yet Muslims now feel only prayer, fasting and zakat.

outline.heading: Who will answer on Judgment Day?
outline.gist: Everyone will be questioned about why the community's problems were not dealt with, and 'ask our leaders' fails when there is no leadership structure.

outline.heading: All of us stand accountable
outline.gist: Drugs, domestic violence, dropouts and lost identity rest on everyone; only someone who contributed their piece can move on, which is why each should take up one category.

outline.heading: Interlude
Education, the only gateway
outline.gist: He offers his five categories while admitting he may be wrong; education is the only gateway for a Muslim society, since ignorance is the mother of all evils.

outline.heading: Mentorship: decent people, no network
outline.gist: Mentorship differs from education: it needs only decent human beings, of whom there are many, but there is no system connecting them.

outline.heading: Financial centralization through incentives
outline.gist: Not his forte, but people need incentives to belong: he holds himself to one standard and offers others incentives; the same 4,000 faces fill the masjids out of some 35,000 Muslims.

outline.heading: Outreach to the 30,000, and advocacy
outline.gist: Some 30,000 local Muslims never come, and non-Muslims too need dawah; advocacy means standing for our rights and others', not party politics; find where your piece fits.

outline.heading: Outro

CZ5XigjEVCc.title: Attributes of the Prophet: Our Following of the Prophet
CZ5XigjEVCc.one_line: Closing the series: Ramadan must bear fruit in following the Prophet, serving his ummah, and five areas the community must invest in.
CZ5XigjEVCc.summary: Closing his Ramadan series on the Prophet's attributes, he argues that worship must produce a visible fruit; otherwise the effort disperses into nothing. The first fruit is following the Prophet honestly, holding ourselves to his standard and learning to think as he thought. The companions used worship as fuel for building the ummah, as night prayer prepared the Prophet for a heavy message, so Ramadan is a beginning, a boot camp, not an end. Nothing should come ahead of Allah and His Messenger, and the believer's horizon must be the state of the Prophet's ummah, whose guidance benefits all people. We must be able to plead before Allah that we tried, like Shuayb seeking reform as far as he could, without judging who will accept. Reflecting on ten years since leaving Syria, he says one belongs by serving and must work wherever Allah has placed him, asking whether anyone benefits from his existence. He proposes five areas for the community: education, outreach to Muslims and non-Muslims, mentorship, financial organisation, and advocacy. He ends with Musa, Yunus and Uthman to show that one big, sincere contribution outweighs small faults, and urges listeners to make Ramadan the start of their story.

outline.heading: Opening
Looking back on the attributes covered
outline.gist: He lists the traits and relationships of the Prophet the series covered, and turns now to our following of him.

outline.heading: Every act of worship must bear fruit
outline.gist: After a month of effort something in character, habits and routine must change, or the energy is lost; ask what the fruit of your worship is.

outline.heading: Follow him to his standard, and think as he thought
outline.gist: The best among us is the one who follows him most; we must imitate not only his behaviour but his way of thinking, and measure ourselves a step closer.

outline.heading: Worship as fuel: night prayer before a heavy word
outline.gist: The companions used worship to power their work for the ummah, just as Allah told the Prophet to pray at night before giving him a heavy message to carry.

outline.heading: Ramadan is a beginning, a boot camp
outline.gist: Things begin with Ramadan; it recentres, trains and strengthens us so we can do the job afterwards.

outline.heading: Nothing ahead of Allah and His Messenger
outline.gist: He is the excellent model for those who seek Allah and the Hereafter; nothing in our priorities comes before them.

outline.heading: Take what he gave you; follow him to be loved
outline.gist: Embrace what he brought and avoid what he forbade; following him is how love of Allah is proven.

outline.heading: The state of his ummah as the goal
outline.gist: Beyond work and the masjid, believers need a long-term vision of the ummah rising again, identifying its gaps and fixing them.

outline.heading: The best nation for all people
outline.gist: The good of this world comes through this ummah's guidance, which serves believers and non-believers alike; like children, people do not always know what is good for them.

outline.heading: An excuse before your Lord
outline.gist: Many Muslims lack concern beyond themselves; like those in the Quran who kept advising a doomed town, we must be able to plead before Allah that we tried.

outline.heading: You do not know who will accept
outline.gist: The masjid never planned for converts yet dozens embraced Islam in a year, mostly brought by young friends; just do your part.

outline.heading: Shuayb: reform as far as I am able
outline.gist: His favourite verse: the aim is reform to the limit of one's capacity.

outline.heading: Belonging by serving
outline.gist: Never fully accepted in Canada, Saudi or Syria, he was told by a teacher that the only way to belong is to serve, and spent fifteen years serving youth in Syria until he was accepted.

outline.heading: Uprooted, and still seeking fruit
outline.gist: Forced to leave after detention, he found measuring progress hard in a new land without degree, network or vocabulary, but ten idle years would be ten wasted years.

outline.heading: Work where Allah put you
outline.gist: Circumstances are never optimal; ask whether anyone benefits from your being alive and push something forward, however small.

outline.heading: Time flies; a bigger goal makes it bearable
outline.gist: Ten years pass in a blink and midlife crises come from refusing that; a goal beyond degree, marriage and house makes the passing of time meaningful.

outline.heading: Community priority: education
outline.gist: Islamic and broader education, skills and the right knowledge at the right life stage, with lifelong learning and narratives youth can defend.

outline.heading: Community priority: outreach
outline.gist: Dawah to Muslims in the grey area who feel unwelcome in masjids, and to non-Muslims, which is the reason for living here.

outline.heading: Community priority: mentorship
outline.gist: Distinct from education: role models who help youth build identity and belonging; university students and professionals must give time, as mentors saved him.

outline.heading: Community priority: financial organisation
outline.gist: The community has wealth but poor management and no centralisation, relying on constant fundraising while masjid budgets lag far behind other faiths.

outline.heading: Community priority: advocacy
outline.gist: Laws should reflect the will of a million Canadian Muslims; the generation born here must reject the keep-your-head-down mentality and organise.

outline.heading: Education and mentorship are not the same
outline.gist: Education needs people of knowledge; mentorship needs decent people willing to give time.

outline.heading: What the Prophet would tell us
outline.gist: The five areas came from asking what he would advise: invest in people and community, with the global ummah as the bigger goal.

outline.heading: Make Ramadan the beginning of your story
outline.gist: Dream big and bring something great to Allah, who could scrutinise every moment but overlooks much for a great deed.

outline.heading: Musa's anger overlooked; Yunus's departure
outline.gist: Musa's throwing of the tablets drew no rebuke because of his stand before Pharaoh despite fear, while Yunus left his people without permission and was tested in the whale.

outline.heading: Uthman: nothing will harm him after today
outline.gist: Uthman equipped an army and bought a well for Madinah; one great deed at the right moment covers later mistakes.

outline.heading: Outro
